title: ADR: Quantization profiles are opt-in and route-scoped (with canary + rollback model)
author: Ravi Menon
content:
## Status
Published.

## Decision owners
- Smart Routing / Platform: Mina Haddad, Ravi Menon
- Serving Runtime: Mateo Alvarez
- Applied ML / Evals: Arjun Desai
- SRE: Sean Gallagher

## Context
Redwood Inference is shipping an opt-in Quantization Profile Library that publishes Redwood-validated quantization profiles per model (e.g., bf16/fp16/int8/int4), scoped to specific hardware and kernel/runtime compatibility constraints.

Quantization provides meaningful cost and latency improvements, but it is not universally safe:
- Quality regressions are workload-specific (e.g., JSON-mode / tool-calling, long-context reasoning, niche domains).
- Runtime + hardware compatibility is non-trivial and can fail in ways that materially impact availability (kernel mismatch, unsupported GPU arch, memory pressure).
- Customer risk tolerance varies; some routes are customer-facing interactive chat with tight quality/format requirements, while others are background batch summarization.

We need a control and rollout model that reduces unit cost without compromising reliability or customer trust.

## Problem statement
We must decide:
1) Whether quantization should be enabled by default or opt-in.
2) Whether controls should be model-scoped only, or route-scoped (and why).
3) The rollout/rollback model that enables safe adoption at scale across Hosted/Dedicated/Private.

## Decision
### 1) Quantization will be opt-in for v1
Quantization profiles will not be automatically applied globally. Customers (or Redwood for internal/system routes) must explicitly enable quantization via route-level configuration.

Default behavior remains baseline (non-quantized) execution.

### 2) Quantization enablement will be route-scoped (with optional higher-level defaults)
Quantization enablement will be configured and evaluated at the **route** level.

We will support a precedence model in the control plane to allow optional defaults:
- Org-level default (optional)
- Customer-level overrides (optional; primarily for enterprise / Dedicated)
- Route-level setting (authoritative for safety and experimentation)

In other words: higher levels may provide defaults, but the intended operational and product “unit of control” is the route.

### 3) Rollout model: canary percentage per route + fast rollback (manual and automated)
We will support:
- Per-route canary percentage (0–100%) to gradually shift traffic to quantized execution.
- Automatic fallback to baseline on incompatibility (runtime/hardware/kernel mismatch).
- Automatic disable on regression signals (quality and reliability thresholds) at the route scope.
- A single-action rollback path: set route quantization to disabled (or canary=0), reverting all traffic to baseline.

## Rationale
### Why opt-in (vs default-on)
1) **Trust and predictability:** Quantization changes the model’s numerical behavior and can alter outputs in subtle ways. Default-on would create “silent changes” for customers who did not request them.
2) **Workload variance:** Regression risk is not uniform. A profile can pass general evals but fail specific formatting constraints, tool-calling, or long-context routes.
3) **Operational blast radius:** Early library versions will have a growing compatibility matrix. Opt-in reduces the probability of broad availability incidents due to mis-scoping or kernel issues.
4) **Clear product contract:** Opt-in makes the performance/cost tradeoff explicit, aligning with Redwood’s “production economics with control” positioning.

### Why route-scoped (vs model-scoped only)
Model-scoped enablement is too coarse for realistic production systems:
- **Different routes have different quality thresholds.** Example: interactive chat route may require strict adherence to JSON schema and consistent tool arguments; a summarization route may tolerate small stylistic changes.
- **Different latency SLOs and load shapes.** Batch routes can accept higher p95 latency if cost decreases; interactive routes generally cannot.
- **Safer experimentation.** Route scoping matches how customers deploy and measure changes (per endpoint/feature), making it easier to canary, compare, and roll back.
- **Reduced blast radius.** A regression should not force disabling quantization for an entire model across the customer’s application.

Route-scoped controls also align with our existing rollout primitives (canary, A/B, fallback policies) and existing routing policy evaluation points.

## Options considered
### Option A: Default-on quantization for all supported models
- Pros: fastest cost reduction; fewer knobs.
- Cons: high risk of quality regressions and incident blast radius; breaks customer expectation of stable model behavior; harder to attribute changes; increased support load.
- Decision: Rejected for v1.

### Option B: Opt-in but model-scoped only
- Pros: simpler configuration surface; fewer evaluation checks.
- Cons: still too coarse; forces “all routes for this model” to share a single risk posture; complicates adoption because customers cannot isolate to safe workloads.
- Decision: Rejected.

### Option C: Opt-in and route-scoped (selected)
- Pros: best safety/control tradeoff; aligns with rollouts; supports per-workload measurement; reduces blast radius.
- Cons: more config complexity; requires robust precedence, validation, and audit logging.
- Decision: Accepted.

### Option D: Request-scoped (per API call) control via headers only
- Pros: maximal flexibility for experimentation.
- Cons: difficult to reason about billing attribution and auditability; can be abused unintentionally; can bypass safety policy; makes stable rollout harder.
- Decision: Not supported as the primary mechanism in v1. (We may allow limited “debug overrides” for internal use with strict RBAC and logging.)

## Rollout & rollback model (normative)
### Configuration primitives
Each route has a quantization setting with:
- enabled: true/false
- canary_percent: 0–100 (evaluated deterministically per request using a stable hash key)
- allow_fallback_to_baseline: true (default)
- pinned_profile_id (optional): used only for debugging or controlled pinning; otherwise profile is resolved by routing/runtime rules

### Evaluation order (high level)
1) Determine route-level policy result (including canary decision).
2) If policy says baseline: execute baseline.
3) If policy says quantized:
   - Resolve compatible quantization profile (model + requested constraints + hardware/kernel scope).
   - If no compatible profile exists or verification fails: fall back to baseline and emit a structured reason.
   - Execute quantized path; tag telemetry with profile id/version.

### Canary mechanics
- Canary assignment must be stable (per org + route + request key) to avoid flapping.
- Default request key: (org_id, route_id, end_user_id) when available; fallback to (org_id, route_id, request_id) if end_user_id is absent.
- Canary is evaluated before runtime resolution to avoid unnecessary profile fetch when canary selects baseline.

### Rollback expectations
Rollback must be effective within minutes:
- Control plane config update propagates to routing policy evaluation quickly (target < 2 minutes for Hosted; Dedicated/Private dependent on deployment but same design intent).
- Runtime must not “stick” to cached profiles when policy disables quantization; policy decision is authoritative.
- Runtime incompatibility fallback is always enabled in v1; it is not a customer-facing toggle.

### Automated disable triggers (route-scoped)
Quantization is automatically disabled (set canary_percent to 0 and/or enabled=false) for a route when any of the following occur (thresholds defined in performance standards; examples below are illustrative):
- Reliability: sustained increase in 5xx rate attributable to quantized path beyond threshold.
- Latency: sustained p95 latency regression beyond threshold for the route’s SLO class.
- Quality: eval harness or online quality monitors signal regression above allowed delta for the route’s tagged prompt sets.

All automatic actions must write an audit log event with:
- actor = system
- route
- previous config
- new config
- triggering signal + window
- link to dashboard/incident

## Consequences
### Positive
- Customers can adopt quantization safely, starting with tolerant workloads.
- Reduced operational blast radius; faster time-to-mitigate.
- Clean measurement: route-level comparison of baseline vs quantized with stable traffic splits.
- Aligns with Redwood’s existing rollout primitives and Console UX mental model.

### Negative / costs
- More complexity in control plane and policy precedence.
- Console/API UX must educate users on canary usage and risks.
- Requires strong telemetry tagging and attribution to avoid confusion in cost/latency dashboards.

## Security, compliance, and auditability
- All config changes (manual or automated) must be auditable and queryable.
- Quantization profile artifacts must be signed and verified during resolution (see threat model).
- Publishing permissions are restricted; library is Redwood-published only in v1.

## Success criteria (for this decision)
- No platform-wide behavior change for customers not opting in.
- Route-level canary enables partial adoption within a customer without support intervention.
- Median time-to-rollback for a quantization-related incident is < 10 minutes from detection to effective disablement.
- Support tickets for “unexpected output change” decrease over time as route scoping is adopted.

## Open questions
- Do we need a first-class “route risk class” tag (interactive vs batch) to set recommended defaults and alert thresholds?
- Should we support profile pinning for enterprise change management (with explicit lifecycle + expiration)?
- How do we represent route-scoped quality gates in Console (mapping routes to prompt sets/evals) without overwhelming users?

## Implementation notes (non-normative)
- Runtime must record quantization execution mode (baseline/quantized/fallback) and the profile id/version on traces and metrics for accurate attribution.
- Policy engine must expose a structured reason when quantization is not applied (disabled, canary not selected, incompatibility, profile missing, verification failure).
